passage: Rain ended the sports period early, so Seema Miss let class five talk cricket in the school hall. Jomon was on his feet at once. "Number 7 is the best batter in the world. Remember his hundred against the Lions? And the sixty in the final?" Seema Miss asked, "What about the last four matches?" Jomon waved a hand. "The first one was the umpire's fault. Then the pitch was wet. Then the sun was in his eyes." A classmate held up the newspaper score card: 3, 0, 11, 5. Jomon folded his arms and shook his head. "That's just bad luck. Real fans know he's the best." A few children giggled, and he glared at them.

qa.q: What did the classmate hold up during the cricket talk?
qa.a: The classmate held up the newspaper score card showing 3, 0, 11 and 5.

qa.q: Why does it feel reasonable to Jomon to blame the umpire, the wet pitch and the sun?
qa.a: Jomon remembers the hundred and the sixty clearly, so the low scores feel like strange accidents rather than real evidence. Admitting them would feel like letting his hero down.

qa.q: What small step could help Jomon see the whole picture?
qa.a: He could write down every score from the season, good and bad, and look at them together before deciding who is best. Seema Miss could ask him to work out the average, which counts every match the same.

qa.q: How might the classmate with the score card see Jomon's reaction?
qa.a: The classmate may feel that no score will ever count as proof for Jomon, which could make talking cricket with him frustrating.

grounding: Shows a boy remembering only his favourite cricketer's big innings and explaining away the low scores as the umpire, the pitch or bad luck.

passage: I'm Nirmala, Gurpreet's didi, and my little brother, who is nine, has one hero: the team's left-arm fast bowler. Our bedroom wall is covered with his pictures. qa.a: He may feel uncomfortable or defensive, because that match doesn't fit the picture of his hero. Saying he doesn't remember lets the happy story stay whole.

qa.a: Papa could sit with him and list every match of the season, the five-wicket day and the costly ones, and ask what the whole list says. Doing it as a shared game keeps Gurpreet from feeling attacked.

qa.q: How does Nirmala see her brother's habit?

passage: Shalini, you think your father was always this calm about cricket? Your grandmother remembers. When Zorama was ten, here in Aizawl, he had one hero, an opening batsman. qa.a: Instead of arguing, Lalremsiami asked him to count the failures and then counted them with him from the sports page. The real number, seven, was hard to ignore.

passage: The Nagpur wedding hall was deafening, and the only way to follow the match was Vidya's phone, which kept losing signal. Her cousin Raghav, nine, pressed against her elbow. passage: Suraj, you think your grandfather was always this calm about cricket? When I was nine, in our Kanpur lane, my hero was an opener called Vinod Pai. I kept a notebook of his scores, but only the big ones. His ninety-eight against the visitors went in with three underlines. When he got out for two, I told everyone the umpire was blind. When he got out for zero, I said the pitch was wet, just bad luck. My friend Hari once brought the newspaper with the whole season printed: more low scores than high. I tore the page and ran home. That evening my father asked, "Kunal, if another batsman had these scores, what would you call him?" I had no answer, and that question stayed with me longer than any match.

qa.q: Why did tearing Hari's newspaper page feel right to young Kunal at the time?
qa.a: He felt threatened and embarrassed, because the page attacked a hero he loved, so defending Vinod Pai felt like loyalty, not like ignoring the facts.

qa.q: Which moment became the turning point for Kunal, and why did it work?
qa.a: His father's question about what he would call another batsman with the same scores; it made him judge the numbers without his love for Vinod Pai in the way.

qa.q: How might Hari have felt when Kunal tore the page?
qa.a: Hari probably felt hurt and frustrated, since he had brought the real scores to share and got an angry friend instead.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, he kept only his favourite batsman's big scores and blamed umpires and luck for the low ones.

passage:
Class 5 note, Friday

During the cricket discussion today, Pradeep told the class his favourite player "never fails." When Vikram mentioned the player's low scores in the last series, Pradeep said, "The umpires were against him. And it rained." When another child mentioned a century, Pradeep lit up and described every shot.

It was clear he only remembered the matches that fit. The rest were bad luck.

I didn't correct him in front of everyone. After class I asked him to fill in a small table from the newspaper: every score in the last ten matches. He was unhappy at first. When he finished, he looked at it for a long time and said, "Maybe he's the best sometimes."

I'll use the same table idea for our maths lesson on averages next week.

— Vidya

qa.a: He felt excited and proud, because the century fit his belief about his hero, so it was the kind of fact he wanted to hear.

qa.q: What was wise about Vidya's table idea?
qa.a: It made Pradeep look at all the scores himself, privately, so he could see the pattern without feeling embarrassed in class.

qa.q: How might Vikram have felt when Pradeep blamed the umpires?
qa.a: Vikram may have felt frustrated or brushed off, since his fact was dismissed.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a boy who insists his favourite cricketer never fails and remembers only the matches that prove it.

Dear Diary,
Monsoon holidays, day 4. Raining AGAIN so no cricket outside.

Watched the old match videos with Ritu didi. I showed her the century by Sameer Khanna, the one where he hit six sixes. Best batsman in the world.

Then she found the match where he got out for zero. I said the umpire was blind. It was clearly not out! Another one, out for 3. I said wet pitch, bad luck.

She said, "Vikas, when your favourite scores, it's talent, and when he doesn't, it's luck?"

I said YES. Because it is.

But now I'm writing this and thinking... maybe I only watch the centuries. I have like 20 saved. I have zero saved of him getting out.

Still best in the world though. Probably.

The paddy had just been cut in Mohit's village and the whole family sat on the threshing ground in the cold Pongal sun, listening to the match on Thatha's radio.

"Karan Rao will score a hundred," Mohit announced. "He always does."

His cousin Seema, peeling sugarcane, laughed. "Always? He got out for nine last week."

"The ball swung. Nobody could play that ball."

"And the week before? Fourteen."

"Wrong decision. Everyone saw." Mohit's ears went hot.

On the radio, Karan Rao edged the second ball to slip. Out for two.

"That was a no-ball! It must be!"

Seema handed him a piece of sugarcane. "Mohit, you remember his hundreds like festival days. The bad days you forget."

He sat down, chewing hard, and didn't answer.

"He's still the greatest," Xin muttered, but quieter.
